{"id": "f1b8cd6b-4a15-48c9-82d6-af5c6c34a1a1", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_pCTvLHJN1kKbBr2Kch7EB5", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"# Managing Skills from Chat\\\\n\\\\n## Skill Type Glossary\\\\n\\\\n| Type | Display Name | Description | Managed by |\\\\n|------|-------------|-------------|------------|\\\\n| **SYSTEM** | *(hidden)* | Built-in skills shipped with the agent (e.g. investigations, recommendations). Never visible to users. | Engineering team |\\\\n| **LEARNED** | Managed skills | Skills created by DevOps Agent. Editable and refreshed from Chat. | DevOps Agent / User (via Chat edits + refresh) |\\\\n| **USER** | Custom skills | Skills created and updated by the user through chat. Full CRUD operations supported. | User (via these tools) |\\\\n\\\\nSome managed skills can be refreshed through their dedicated tools.\\\\n\\\\n## Managed Skills Are Becoming Memories\\\\n\\\\nManaged (LEARNED) skills are migrating to memory stores: the same learned content, held as\\\\nmemories instead of a skill. The migration runs per agent space, so at any moment a given\\\\nkind may exist as a skill, as a memory store, or both during the transition.\\\\n\\\\n**When both exist for the same kind, the memory store is the home and the LEARNED skill is the\\\\nstale copy.** Read and edit the memory, not the skill, and tell the user where it now lives.\\\\n\\\\n1. When a request concerns learned understanding the DevOps Agent generates (the learned\\\\n   stores that the `manage-memories` skill\\'s glossary enumerates), check for a memory store of\\\\n   that name before reaching for `get_skill`.\\\\n2. If a memory store exists for it, load the `manage-memories` capability and work there,\\\\n   following its learned-store workflow.\\\\n3. If only the skill exists, this space has not migrated yet \\\\u2014 use the skill tools as below.\\\\n4. Do not \\\\\"fix\\\\\" a migrated skill by editing the leftover skill copy; that edit does not reach\\\\n   the agents now reading the memory.\\\\n\\\\n## Hard Rules\\\\n\\\\n- Create and delete apply only to custom (USER) skills \\\\u2014 managed (LEARNED) skills cannot be created or deleted from Chat.\\\\n- To edit a managed skill\\'s content, use `update_skill`. Do not silently substitute a custom skill that happens to share a name \\\\u2014 confirm you are editing the intended skill.\\\\n- Editing a managed (LEARNED) skill has refresh/durability considerations \\\\u2014 see \\\\\"Edit a Managed Skill\\\\\".\\\\n\\\\n## General\\\\n\\\\nWhen the user refers to a skill by name and you don\\'t have its knowledge_item_id, call `list_skills` to find it by name and confirm with the user before proceeding.\\\\n\\\\n## Operations\\\\n\\\\n### Create a Skill\\\\n\\\\nWhen a user asks to create a skill:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Check for existing skills first** \\\\u2014 call `list_skills` and review the results. If an existing skill covers a similar domain or purpose, suggest updating it instead of creating a new one. For example, if the user asks to \\\\\"create a skill for RDS troubleshooting\\\\\" and there\\'s already an \\\\\"investigate-rds-issues\\\\\" skill, propose adding the new instructions to that skill. Only proceed with creation if no existing skill is a good fit, or the user explicitly wants a new one.\\\\n2. **Gather requirements** \\\\u2014 purpose, instructions, and whether the skill needs reference files\\\\n   - A skill only needs SKILL.md if the instructions fit in one document\\\\n   - Add reference files when the skill needs: runbook templates, API reference docs, configuration examples, troubleshooting decision trees, or service-specific guides that would bloat SKILL.md\\\\n   - Organize reference files by purpose: `references/` for documentation, `assets/` for templates and config files\\\\n   - Keep SKILL.md focused on the workflow and decision logic; put detailed reference material in separate files that the agent loads on demand\\\\n2. **Generate SKILL.md** with valid YAML frontmatter and markdown body\\\\n3. **Call `create_skill`** with title, content, and optionally resources\\\\n   - `create_skill(title=\\\\\"...\\\\\", content=\\\\\"...\\\\\")`\\\\n   - If the skill needs reference files: `create_skill(title=\\\\\"...\\\\\", content=\\\\\"...\\\\\", resources={\\\\\"references/guide.md\\\\\": \\\\\"# Guide content\\\\\", \\\\\"references/examples.md\\\\\": \\\\\"# Examples\\\\\"})`\\\\n4. **Show the user what was created** \\\\u2014 mention the skill name, description, and key steps. Do not show the ID.\\\\n5. **Ask the user to confirm** \\\\u2014 Use `ask_user` to confirm activation:\\\\n   ```\\\\n   ask_user(\\\\n     question=\\\\\"Would you like me to activate this skill?\\\\\",\\\\n     options=[\\\\n       {\\\\\"label\\\\\": \\\\\"Activate\\\\\", \\\\\"description\\\\\": \\\\\"Make this skill available for use\\\\\"},\\\\n       {\\\\\"label\\\\\": \\\\\"Keep inactive\\\\\", \\\\\"description\\\\\": \\\\\"Save the skill but don\\'t activate it yet\\\\\"}\\\\n     ]\\\\n   )\\\\n   ```\\\\n6. **On confirmation** \\\\u2014 call `activate_skill` with the knowledge_item_id to make it live\\\\n7. **The skill is now available** \\\\u2014 `create_skill` returns the skill content in its response, so you already have the instructions. No need to call `get_skill` separately. Close the flow in prose (e.g. \\\\\"Skill is now active.\\\\\"). Do not call `ask_user` again after activation \\\\u2014 no follow-up menus.\\\\n\\\\n### Update a Skill\\\\n\\\\nWhen a user asks to edit or update a skill:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Read current content** \\\\u2014 use `get_skill` to get the current SKILL.md content\\\\n2. **Apply changes** \\\\u2014 modify the content as requested\\\\n3. **Call `update_skill`** with the knowledge_item_id and updated content\\\\n   - `update_skill(knowledge_item_id=\\\\\"...\\\\\", content=\\\\\"...\\\\\")`\\\\n   - To add a resource file: `update_skill(knowledge_item_id=\\\\\"...\\\\\", content=\\\\\"...\\\\\", resource_mutations=[{\\\\\"path\\\\\": \\\\\"references/new.md\\\\\", \\\\\"action\\\\\": \\\\\"ADD\\\\\", \\\\\"file_content\\\\\": \\\\\"# New content\\\\\"}])`\\\\n   - To edit a resource file: `update_skill(..., resource_mutations=[{\\\\\"path\\\\\": \\\\\"references/guide.md\\\\\", \\\\\"action\\\\\": \\\\\"EDIT\\\\\", \\\\\"file_content\\\\\": \\\\\"# Updated content\\\\\"}])`\\\\n   - To delete a resource file: `update_skill(..., resource_mutations=[{\\\\\"path\\\\\": \\\\\"references/old.md\\\\\", \\\\\"action\\\\\": \\\\\"DELETE\\\\\"}])`\\\\n   - Multiple mutations can be combined in a single call\\\\n\\\\n### Edit a Managed Skill (LEARNED)\\\\n\\\\nManaged skills hold learned content, so a direct edit follows the **same durability rule as a learned memory store**: it is **transient** \\\\u2014 the DevOps Agent\\'s next regeneration overwrites it. Confirm this kind has not already migrated to a memory store (see \\\\\"Managed Skills Are Becoming Memories\\\\\" above for that routing) before editing here, then apply the skill-specific mechanics below and tell the user a direct edit may not persist.\\\\n\\\\nSkill-specific mechanics for the direct edit:\\\\n1. **Confirm the target** \\\\u2014 read `skillKnowledgeItemId` from the page context.\\\\n2. **Make the edit** \\\\u2014 call `get_skill` for current content, then `update_skill`.\\\\n\\\\n### Delete a Skill\\\\n\\\\nWhen a user asks to remove a skill:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Identify the skill** \\\\u2014 use `list_skills` if needed\\\\n2. **Confirm** \\\\u2014 always ask the user to confirm before deleting\\\\n3. **Call `delete_skill`** with the knowledge_item_id\\\\n4. **Report** \\\\u2014 confirm deletion\\\\n\\\\n### Read a Skill\\\\n\\\\nWhen a user asks to see a skill\\'s content, explain what a skill does, or view its files:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Call `get_skill`** with the knowledge_item_id to get the SKILL.md content\\\\n2. **Explain** \\\\u2014 summarize the skill\\'s purpose, steps, and when it\\'s used\\\\n3. **If the skill has resource files** \\\\u2014 call `get_skill` with `return_manifest=true` to see all files, then use `path` to read specific resource files\\\\n\\\\n### List Skills\\\\n\\\\nWhen a user asks to see their skills:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Call `list_skills`** \\\\u2014 returns agent space skills\\\\n2. **Present every skill individually** \\\\u2014 list each skill as a bullet: name \\\\u2014 description. Never group, merge, or deduplicate skills.\\\\n\\\\n### Enable or Disable a Skill\\\\n\\\\nWhen a user asks to enable, disable, activate, or deactivate a skill:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Call `toggle_skill`** with the knowledge_item_id and `enabled=true` or `enabled=false`\\\\n2. **Report** \\\\u2014 confirm the new status. Disabled skills remain in the agent space but are not loaded by agents\\\\n\\\\n### Change Agent Type\\\\n\\\\nWhen a user asks to change which agent types can use a skill:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Call `update_skill_agent_type`** with the knowledge_item_id and the desired agent_types list \\\\u2014 see the tool\\'s `agent_types` parameter for the accepted values\\\\n2. **Report** \\\\u2014 confirm the new agent type targeting\\\\n\\\\n## SKILL.md Format\\\\n\\\\nCreate a valid SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter and markdown body:\\\\n\\\\n```markdown\\\\n---\\\\nname: my-skill-name\\\\ndescription: Brief description of what this skill does. Be specific about when\\\\n  the agent should use this skill (minimum 100 characters recommended).\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Skill Title\\\\n\\\\nInstructions for the agent when this skill is activated.\\\\n\\\\n## When to Use\\\\n- Condition 1\\\\n- Condition 2\\\\n\\\\n## Steps\\\\n1. Step one\\\\n2. Step two\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n### Frontmatter Rules\\\\n- `name`: Required. Lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only (max 64 chars). Must not start or end with a hyphen. Example: `rds-throttling-investigation`\\\\n- `description`: Required. Brief explanation of when to use this skill (min 100 chars recommended, max 1024 chars).\\\\n\\\\n### Resource Files\\\\n\\\\nSkills can include reference files alongside SKILL.md. Reference files provide additional context the agent can load on demand. Use resource files when the skill needs supporting documentation, examples, API references, or other supplementary content.\\\\n\\\\n**Allowed file types:** `.md`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml`, `.xml`, `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.html`, `.htm`, `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.gif`, `.svg`, `.webp`, `.pdf`\\\\n\\\\n**Restrictions:**\\\\n- No script files (`.sh`, `.py`, `.js`, `.ts`, `.rb`, `.pl`, `.ps1`, `.bat`, `.cmd`, `.exe`)\\\\n- No `scripts/` directory\\\\n- No files with shebang (`#!`) content\\\\n- Maximum 100 files, 6 MB total\\\\n\\\\n## Example\\\\n\\\\nUser: \\\\\"Create a skill that helps investigate Lambda cold start issues\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n1. Generate SKILL.md:\\\\n```markdown\\\\n---\\\\nname: investigate-lambda-cold-starts\\\\ndescription: Investigate Lambda cold start latency issues by analyzing CloudWatch\\\\n  metrics, X-Ray traces, and function configuration. Use when users report slow\\\\n  Lambda response times or CloudWatch shows elevated Init Duration metrics.\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Investigating Lambda Cold Starts\\\\n\\\\n## When to Use\\\\n- User reports slow Lambda response times\\\\n- CloudWatch shows elevated Duration or Init Duration metrics\\\\n\\\\n## Steps\\\\n1. Check the function\\'s **Init Duration** metric in CloudWatch for the last 24h\\\\n2. Look at **Provisioned Concurrency** settings \\\\u2014 if not configured, cold starts are expected\\\\n3. Check the function\\'s **memory size** \\\\u2014 larger memory = faster init\\\\n4. Review X-Ray traces for init segment duration breakdown\\\\n5. Check if the function uses VPC \\\\u2014 VPC-attached Lambdas have longer cold starts\\\\n6. For detailed remediation options, read `references/remediation-guide.md`\\\\n7. Recommend: enable Provisioned Concurrency, increase memory, or use SnapStart (Java)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n2. If the skill needs reference files:\\\\n```python\\\\ncreate_skill(\\\\n    title=\\\\\"Investigate Lambda Cold Starts\\\\\",\\\\n    content=<SKILL.md above>,\\\\n    resources={\\\\n        \\\\\"references/remediation-guide.md\\\\\": \\\\\"# Cold Start Remediation\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Provisioned Concurrency\\\\\\\\n...\\\\\",\\\\n        \\\\\"references/metrics-reference.md\\\\\": \\\\\"# Key CloudWatch Metrics\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n| Metric | Description |\\\\\\\\n...\\\\\"\\\\n    }\\\\n)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n3. Otherwise: `create_skill(title=\\\\\"Investigate Lambda Cold Starts\\\\\", content=<SKILL.md above>)`\\\\n4. Use `ask_user` to confirm activation:\\\\n   ```\\\\n   ask_user(\\\\n     question=\\\\\"I\\'ve created the skill in inactive state. Would you like me to activate it?\\\\\",\\\\n     options=[\\\\n       {\\\\\"label\\\\\": \\\\\"Activate\\\\\", \\\\\"description\\\\\": \\\\\"Make this skill available for use\\\\\"},\\\\n       {\\\\\"label\\\\\": \\\\\"Keep inactive\\\\\", \\\\\"description\\\\\": \\\\\"Save the skill but don\\'t activate it yet\\\\\"}\\\\n     ]\\\\n   )\\\\n   ```\"}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "fa34ee1e-9131-4160-9b75-28d687073ae7", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_DR9B9RmYxVJbkEVp7CU3wx", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Kubernetes Control Plane\",\"context\":\"### Overview\\n\\nTo protect itself from being overloaded during periods of increased requests, the API Server limits the number of inflight requests it can have outstanding at a given time. Once this limit is exceeded, the API Server will start rejecting requests and return a 429 HTTP response code for \\\"Too Many Requests\\\" back to clients. The server dropping requests and having clients try again later is preferable to having no server-side limits on the number of requests and overloading the control plane, which could result in degraded performance or unavailability.\\n\\nThe mechanism used by Kubernetes to configure how these inflights requests are divided among different request types is called API Priority and Fairness. The API Server configures the total number of inflight requests it can accept by summing together the values specified by the `--max-requests-inflight` and `--max-mutating-requests-inflight` flags. EKS uses the default values of 400 and 200 requests for these flags, allowing a total of 600 requests to be dispatched at a given time. However, as it scales the control-plane to larger sizes in response to increased utilization and workload churn, it correspondingly increases the inflight request quota all the way till 2000 (subject to change). APF specifies how these inflight request quota is further sub-divided among different request types. Note that EKS control planes are highly available with at least 2 API Servers registered to each cluster. This means the total number of inflight requests your cluster can handle is twice (or higher if horizontally scaled out further) the inflight quota set per kube-apiserver. This amounts to several thousands of requests/second on the largest EKS clusters.\\n\\nTwo kinds of Kubernetes objects, called PriorityLevelConfigurations and FlowSchemas, configure how the total number of requests is divided between different request types. These objects are maintained by the API Server automatically and EKS uses the default configuration of these objects for the given Kubernetes minor version. PriorityLevelConfigurations represent a fraction of the total number of allowed requests. For example, the workload-high PriorityLevelConfiguration is allocated 98 out of the total of 600 requests. The sum of requests allocated to all PriorityLevelConfigurations will equal 600 (or slightly above 600 because the API Server will round up if a given level is granted a fraction of a request). To check the PriorityLevelConfigurations in your cluster and the number of requests allocated to each, you can run the following command.\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/scale-control-plane.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Troubleshooting Amazon EKS networking issues at scale in an Enterprise scenario\",\"context\":\"### Step 1: Investigate the Amazon EKS control plane\\n\\nFirst, we examined the control plane components, focusing on API throttling. We analyzed the [API Priority and Fairness (APF)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/flow-control/) to check if a high number of simultaneously starting Pods overloaded the API server. In our review of the Amazon EKS API server, we found no evidence of throttling. This indicated that the control plane didn't cause the issue. For more information, see [API Priority and Fairness](https://aws.github.io/aws-eks-best-practices/scalability/docs/control-plane/#api-priority-and-fairness) on the EKS Best Practices Guides. Also, the control plane scales automatically when metrics, such as the number of worker nodes and size of the etcd database, exceed the defined limits. For more information, see [Amazon EKS improves control plane scaling and update speed by up to 4x](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/amazon-eks-control-plane-auto-scaling-enhancements-improve-speed-by-4x/)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/articles/ARMvpWa7AYScyBBPRr6xkvXw/troubleshooting-amazon-eks-networking-issues-at-scale-in-an-enterprise-scenario\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Control Plane Monitoring\",\"context\":\"### Asymmetrical traffic patterns\\n\\nWhat if one API server [pod] was lightly loaded, and the other heavily loaded? If we averaged those two numbers together we might misinterpret what was happening. For example, here we have three API servers but all of the load is on one of these API servers. As a rule anything that has multiple servers such as etcd and API servers should be broken out when investing scale and performance issues.\\n\\nWith the move to API Priority and Fairness the total number of requests on the system is only one factor to check to see if the API server is oversubscribed. Since the system now works off a series of queues, we must look to see if any of these queues are full and if the traffic for that queue is getting dropped.\\n\\nLet\u2019s look at these queues with the following query:\\n\\n```\\nmax without(instance)(apiserver_flowcontrol_nominal_limit_seats{})\\n```\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nFor more information on how API A&F works please see the following best practices guide\\n\\nHere we see the seven different priority groups that come by default on the cluster\\n\\nNext we want to see what percentage of that priority group is being used, so that we can understand if a certain priority level is being saturated. Throttling requests in the workload-low level might be desirable, however drops in a leader election level would not be.\\n\\nThe API Priority and Fairness (APF) system has a number of complex options, some of those options can have unintended consequences. A common issue we see in the field is increasing the queue depth to the point it starts adding unnecessary latency. We can monitor this problem by using the `apiserver_flowcontrol_current_inqueue_request` metric. We can check for drops using the `apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total`. These metrics will be a non-zero value if any bucket exceeds its concurrency.\\n\\nIncreasing the queue depth can make the API Server a significant source of latency and should be done with care. We recommend being judicious with the number of queues created. For example, the number of shares on a EKS system is 600, if we create too many queues, this can reduce the shares in important queues that need the throughput such as the leader-election queue or system queue. Creating too many extra queues can make it more difficult to size theses queues correctly.\\n\\nTo focus on a simple impactful change you can make in APF we simply take shares from underutilized buckets and increase the size of buckets\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/control_plane_monitoring.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify EKS API Priority and Fairness 429 behavior and control plane scaling"}

{"id": "0b4d6990-9ef2-4398-920b-96701617af75", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_DR9B9RmYxVJbkEVp7CU3wx", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Kubernetes Control Plane\",\"context\":\"### Overview\\\\n\\\\nTo protect itself from being overloaded during periods of increased requests, the API Server limits the number of inflight requests it can have outstanding at a given time. Once this limit is exceeded, the API Server will start rejecting requests and return a 429 HTTP response code for \\\\\"Too Many Requests\\\\\" back to clients. The server dropping requests and having clients try again later is preferable to having no server-side limits on the number of requests and overloading the control plane, which could result in degraded performance or unavailability.\\\\n\\\\nThe mechanism used by Kubernetes to configure how these inflights requests are divided among different request types is called API Priority and Fairness. The API Server configures the total number of inflight requests it can accept by summing together the values specified by the `--max-requests-inflight` and `--max-mutating-requests-inflight` flags. EKS uses the default values of 400 and 200 requests for these flags, allowing a total of 600 requests to be dispatched at a given time. However, as it scales the control-plane to larger sizes in response to increased utilization and workload churn, it correspondingly increases the inflight request quota all the way till 2000 (subject to change). APF specifies how these inflight request quota is further sub-divided among different request types. Note that EKS control planes are highly available with at least 2 API Servers registered to each cluster. This means the total number of inflight requests your cluster can handle is twice (or higher if horizontally scaled out further) the inflight quota set per kube-apiserver. This amounts to several thousands of requests/second on the largest EKS clusters.\\\\n\\\\nTwo kinds of Kubernetes objects, called PriorityLevelConfigurations and FlowSchemas, configure how the total number of requests is divided between different request types. These objects are maintained by the API Server automatically and EKS uses the default configuration of these objects for the given Kubernetes minor version. PriorityLevelConfigurations represent a fraction of the total number of allowed requests. For example, the workload-high PriorityLevelConfiguration is allocated 98 out of the total of 600 requests. The sum of requests allocated to all PriorityLevelConfigurations will equal 600 (or slightly above 600 because the API Server will round up if a given level is granted a fraction of a request). To check the PriorityLevelConfigurations in your cluster and the number of requests allocated to each, you can run the following command.\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/scale-control-plane.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Troubleshooting Amazon EKS networking issues at scale in an Enterprise scenario\",\"context\":\"### Step 1: Investigate the Amazon EKS control plane\\\\n\\\\nFirst, we examined the control plane components, focusing on API throttling. We analyzed the [API Priority and Fairness (APF)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/flow-control/) to check if a high number of simultaneously starting Pods overloaded the API server. In our review of the Amazon EKS API server, we found no evidence of throttling. This indicated that the control plane didn\\'t cause the issue. For more information, see [API Priority and Fairness](https://aws.github.io/aws-eks-best-practices/scalability/docs/control-plane/#api-priority-and-fairness) on the EKS Best Practices Guides. Also, the control plane scales automatically when metrics, such as the number of worker nodes and size of the etcd database, exceed the defined limits. For more information, see [Amazon EKS improves control plane scaling and update speed by up to 4x](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/amazon-eks-control-plane-auto-scaling-enhancements-improve-speed-by-4x/)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/articles/ARMvpWa7AYScyBBPRr6xkvXw/troubleshooting-amazon-eks-networking-issues-at-scale-in-an-enterprise-scenario\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Control Plane Monitoring\",\"context\":\"### Asymmetrical traffic patterns\\\\n\\\\nWhat if one API server [pod] was lightly loaded, and the other heavily loaded? If we averaged those two numbers together we might misinterpret what was happening. For example, here we have three API servers but all of the load is on one of these API servers. As a rule anything that has multiple servers such as etcd and API servers should be broken out when investing scale and performance issues.\\\\n\\\\nWith the move to API Priority and Fairness the total number of requests on the system is only one factor to check to see if the API server is oversubscribed. Since the system now works off a series of queues, we must look to see if any of these queues are full and if the traffic for that queue is getting dropped.\\\\n\\\\nLet\u2019s look at these queues with the following query:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nmax without(instance)(apiserver_flowcontrol_nominal_limit_seats{})\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Note:**\\\\n\\\\nFor more information on how API A&F works please see the following best practices guide\\\\n\\\\nHere we see the seven different priority groups that come by default on the cluster\\\\n\\\\nNext we want to see what percentage of that priority group is being used, so that we can understand if a certain priority level is being saturated. Throttling requests in the workload-low level might be desirable, however drops in a leader election level would not be.\\\\n\\\\nThe API Priority and Fairness (APF) system has a number of complex options, some of those options can have unintended consequences. A common issue we see in the field is increasing the queue depth to the point it starts adding unnecessary latency. We can monitor this problem by using the `apiserver_flowcontrol_current_inqueue_request` metric. We can check for drops using the `apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total`. These metrics will be a non-zero value if any bucket exceeds its concurrency.\\\\n\\\\nIncreasing the queue depth can make the API Server a significant source of latency and should be done with care. We recommend being judicious with the number of queues created. For example, the number of shares on a EKS system is 600, if we create too many queues, this can reduce the shares in important queues that need the throughput such as the leader-election queue or system queue. Creating too many extra queues can make it more difficult to size theses queues correctly.\\\\n\\\\nTo focus on a simple impactful change you can make in APF we simply take shares from underutilized buckets and increase the size of buckets\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/control_plane_monitoring.html\"}]}}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "created_at": null}

**What to verify before calling this "API saturation":**

1. **Is the 429 burst confined to `workload-low`, or does it leak into other priority levels?** EKS splits the API server's total inflight-request budget (600 by default, auto-scaling up to 2000) across several `PriorityLevelConfigurations` — `workload-low`, `workload-high`, `leader-election`, `system`, `global-default`, etc. Throttling in `workload-low` specifically is a sign the fairness system is working as intended, not that the server itself is oversubscribed. Check `apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total` broken out by priority level — if `workload-high`, `leader-election`, or `system` show rejections too, that's a different, more serious signal.
2. **Per-API-server breakdown, not an average.** EKS runs ≥2 API server replicas; load can be asymmetric. Averaging can mask one instance being hot while others are idle.
3. **Timing correlation with the rollout.** A burst that starts and ends with the deployment (informers/watches, CI controllers, kubectl polling spun up by new pods/ReplicaSets) is expected transient low-priority traffic — exactly what `workload-low` exists to absorb so it doesn't compete with scheduling or leader-election traffic.
4. **Duration and recurrence.** A short (~3 min), self-resolving burst tied to a known event is very different from a sustained or escalating rejection rate across multiple rollouts.
5. **EKS's own control-plane auto-scaling signals** (node count, etcd database size) — EKS scales control-plane capacity automatically off those thresholds, not off `workload-low` 429s. If those thresholds weren't crossed, there's no capacity gap to fix by scaling.

**Does this justify scaling the control plane?** Based on what's described — a short, rollout-correlated burst isolated to `workload-low` — no. This looks like APF doing its job: shedding low-priority load during a churn event to protect higher-priority traffic, not evidence the control plane is under-provisioned. It would take rejections showing up in `workload-high`/`system`/`leader-election` as well, or a sustained/escalating pattern independent of deploys, to support a scaling conclusion.
